title: Public Money for Stadiums
resolution: Resolved: Cities should not use public funds to build professional sports stadiums.
summary: Cities often help pay for stadiums to keep or attract teams. Most economists say the local economic payoff is small. Are there other reasons the spending is worth it?

background.p: State and local governments have spent billions of dollars helping build stadiums and arenas for professional teams, through direct spending, bonds, tax breaks and infrastructure. Teams often seek new venues when leases end, and cities compete to keep or attract them.

Economists have studied these deals for decades and largely agree that the local economic benefits are small compared with the public cost: in a 2005 survey of American Economic Association members, 85% agreed governments should eliminate subsidies to professional sports, and in a 2017 University of Chicago panel of economists, 80% agreed stadium subsidies likely cost taxpayers more than the local economic benefits. Supporters respond that teams bring civic pride and quality-of-life benefits that economic studies don't fully capture, and that a stadium can anchor redevelopment of a neighborhood.

disputed.q: How much are a team's non-economic benefits worth to residents?
positions: Supporters cite civic pride, shared identity and studies showing residents value having a team.
Critics say these benefits are real but usually far smaller than the subsidies, and stadiums also bring traffic and other costs.

terms.def: Public money or tax breaks given to support a private business.
Spending at a stadium often replaces other local entertainment spending rather than adding new spending.
Something many people can enjoy at once, like civic pride, that markets may underprovide.
Money a government borrows and repays with interest over time.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: Stadium subsidies cost taxpayers far more than they return; private owners should pay.

args.claim: Studies find little local economic growth from stadiums.
args.warrant: Families have limited entertainment budgets; money spent at games is mostly money not spent at local restaurants, movies or bowling alleys, so total spending barely changes.
args.evidence: Decades of studies reviewed by economists such as John Charles Bradbury and Brad Humphreys; the 2017 University of Chicago economists' panel.
args.response: The negative answers that economic studies miss civic and quality-of-life benefits residents clearly value.

args.warrant: Public dollars spent on a stadium could fund schools, roads, parks or lower taxes, which benefit more residents.
args.evidence: City budget comparisons; the size of recent stadium deals.
args.response: The negative replies that some stadium funding comes from visitor taxes and wouldn't otherwise be available for schools.

args.claim: Teams use the threat of moving to extract money.
args.warrant: Leagues limit the number of teams, so cities bid against each other, and team owners capture the public money.
args.evidence: Histories of team relocations and threats; economists' analyses of league structure.
args.response: The negative argues that a city that refuses may actually lose its team, and with it real civic value.

args.claim: Owners can pay for their own buildings.
args.warrant: Teams and leagues earn large revenues from media, tickets and sponsorships; privately financed stadiums show it can be done.
args.evidence: Examples of privately financed stadiums; team valuation data.
args.response: The negative replies that private financing is rare, and some cities have negotiated public returns such as revenue sharing.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Cities can reasonably invest in stadiums for the civic value teams bring and for redevelopment.

args.claim: Teams bring civic value that money studies miss.
args.warrant: A team gives a city shared identity, pride and something to celebrate together; residents who never attend still enjoy following it.
args.evidence: Contingent-valuation studies of residents' willingness to pay for teams; surveys of civic pride.
args.response: The affirmative answers that economists who study this find these values are usually much smaller than the subsidies.

args.warrant: Well-planned districts with housing, shops and transit around a venue can revive underused areas that private investment alone wouldn't.
args.evidence: Case studies of mixed-use stadium districts; city development reports.
args.response: The affirmative replies that the record of such districts is mixed, and the same money could fund redevelopment directly.

args.claim: Visitors pay part of the cost.
args.warrant: Hotel and rental-car taxes collect money mostly from out-of-towners, so residents bear less of the cost.
args.evidence: Financing structures of recent stadium deals.
args.response: The affirmative answers that those taxes could fund other public needs, so they still have an opportunity cost.

args.claim: Cities can bargain for a fair deal.
args.warrant: Instead of refusing outright, cities can demand revenue sharing, community benefits and ownership of the building, getting real returns.
args.evidence: Stadium agreements with public revenue sharing or community benefit agreements.
args.response: The affirmative argues that with leagues limiting teams, cities rarely have the bargaining power to get fair terms.

strawmen.strawman: They hate sports and want teams to leave.
strawmen.why: Supporters of the resolution can love their teams and still want owners to pay for stadiums.
strawmen.steelman: Economists find stadiums return little local growth for their cost; public money has better uses, and owners can finance their own buildings.

strawmen.strawman: They want to hand billionaires free money.
strawmen.why: Defenders point to civic value, redevelopment and deals that share returns with the public.
strawmen.steelman: Teams bring civic value residents care about, stadiums can anchor redevelopment, visitors pay part of the cost, and cities can negotiate fair returns.

weak.why: Too absolute; the strongest argument is that benefits are small relative to cost.

weak.arg: A new stadium will create thousands of permanent jobs.
weak.why: Most stadium jobs are seasonal and part-time; economists' studies contradict large job claims.

aff: If your city refuses, and the team leaves, what does the city lose?
Do residents value a team even if they never attend?
What about stadiums funded by tourist taxes?
neg: What do surveys of economists say about stadium subsidies?
Why doesn't stadium spending add much to the local economy?
Would the team really leave? Where would it go?
